label: Introduction to Modern IT
headline: Understand what computers actually do before you decide what to do with them.
lede: A nine-module course on the whole IT landscape, written by someone who has spent five decades in it. No coding. No jargon for its own sake. Just what the technology is, what it is good at, what it is bad at, and where it fits in a business.
quote: Most people working around IT have never been told how the pieces fit together. That is not their fault. Nobody wrote it down for them.
audience: Starting an IT apprenticeship, or about to, and wanting the whole picture underneath the specialism rather than after it.
Coming to IT from another field, or coming back after time away, and needing the grounding nobody ever gave you.
Teaching the subject, or hiring into it, and wanting one coherent account of the field rather than ten disconnected ones.
modulesLede: Each module stands on its own. Taken together they build the map of modern computing that most people are expected to already have.
modules: How to get the most from the course
What computers are good at, and what they are not
The parts, and how they fit together
How IT work is planned and delivered
Keeping systems running, day in, day out
Eleven specialisms, from the cloud to the mainframe
Why IT projects succeed, and why so many fail
Staying up, and recovering when you do not
The rules the industry works to
authorLede: Five decades in enterprise computing, and four books on it. The course exists because the same gap kept appearing: capable people, working in and around IT, who had never been given the whole picture.
authorNote: Fifty years in the field, four books, and one conclusion: the people who last in IT are the ones who understand the whole environment, not the ones who know one language very well.
